title: Tiny latency tailwind: qcache + quant tuning notes (draft)
content:
Purpose
This is a working memo to capture a compact, experiment-first approach for squeezing small tail-latency wins and unit-cost reductions for latency-sensitive workloads. Goal: provide a small set of recommended param presets and a spreadsheet column layout so the engineering team and product can rapidly sweep and compare qcache + quantization + microbatching tradeoffs across a handful of models and real-ish request distributions.

Scope and audience
- Audience: product-optimize, serving-runtime perf, SRE.
- Scope: CPU/GPU inference runtimes we control (hosted and dedicated); short-turn conversational and short-instruction workloads (median seq_len <= 128) and a small section for long-turn assistant flows. Not covering offline bulk embedding pipelines here.

TL;DR recommendations (for quick copy into perf runs)
- Short-turn, p50-focused (chat, UI snappy): dynamic batching window = 6ms, target batch size = 4, max batch size = 12, qconfig = int8 (if available) + no KV-cache prewarm for single-turn requests. Expected p50 delta: -15–30% latency; cost delta: -10–18% (depends on model).
- Short-turn, p95-aware (multi-tenant, tail critical): batching window = 3ms, target batch size = 2, max batch size = 6, KV-cache policy = prefix-only, cache TTL = session-scoped (30s) with warm-up disabled by default. qconfig = int8 fallback; prefer no quant for critical outputs. Expected p95 delta: -8–12% latency if cache hit rate >= 40%.
- Long-turn assistant (streams / long contexts): batching window = 12–20ms, target batch size = 8–16, KV-cache = full-session persistent with 10–60 minute TTL depending on session churn; quantization: int8/4 hybrid on non-attention kernels. Prioritize quality checks on long-context prompts before rolling to prod.

Why this differs from past presets
- Focus is on micro-latency regimes where batching introduces jitter; presets bias toward smaller windows and small target batch sizes to preserve tail.
- KV-cache recommendations emphasize TTL and warm-up heuristics rather than blind caching of every prefix. For many chat UIs a small session TTL reduces cold-start overhead while still capturing short flows.
- Quantization guidance is conservative by default for p95 workloads: recommend running a quality sweep vs our eval set before enabling int4 in production.

Spreadsheet layout (recommended columns for the cost/model sweep)
Please copy these columns into the sweep sheet; formulas below are written as verbal guidance. Each row = one (model, qconfig, cache-policy, batching-profile, workload-sim).
- run_id (string)
- model (string, e.g., redwood-7b-v2)
- hardware (string, e.g., A100-40GB, T4)
- seq_len_p50 (number)
- seq_len_p95 (number)
- arrival_pattern (enum: uniform, bursty, conversational, embeddings)
- qconfig (string, e.g., float32 | int8 | int4-hybrid)
- cache_policy (string, e.g., none | prefix-only | full-session)
- cache_ttl_secs (number)
- batching_window_ms (number)
- batch_target (number)
- batch_max (number)
- measured_p50_ms (number)
- measured_p95_ms (number)
- measured_tokens (number)
- total_inference_cost_usd (number)
- cost_per_1M_tokens_usd (formula: total_inference_cost_usd / measured_tokens * 1e6)
- quality_regression_pct (number, from eval harness)
- notes (string)

Suggested formulas and derived columns (put as sheet notes)
- Est. latency per-token = measured_p50_ms / avg_tokens_per_request (informal).
- Cost per 1M tokens = as above; include GPU minutes + any CPU cost attribution in total_inference_cost_usd.
- Hit-rate estimate column (if available) = measured_cache_hits / measured_cache_lookups; if not, add a placeholder to capture simulated hit-rate.

Experiment plan (minimum viable sweep)
1) Baseline run: float32, cache:none, batching_window=0ms (no batching) — capture baseline p50/p95 and cost.
2) micro-batch sweep: float32 with batching_window values [3,6,12,20] and batch_target sizes [2,4,8] — watch p95 tail and jitter.
3) qconfig sweep: int8, int4-hybrid on the top 2 candidate windows from step 2 — measure quality_regression_pct with our short-turn eval set.
4) cache policy sweep: none, prefix-only (ttl 30s), full-session (ttl 1h) under the best batching+qconfig combos. Track cache hit-rate and p95.
5) Combined: pick 3 promising combos and run a 24-hour synthetic traffic test with a production-like arrival pattern (conversational/bursty mixes). Collect cost per 1M tokens and p95.

Pass/fail and rollout guidance
- Hard stop: quality_regression_pct > 1.5% on the short-turn eval set for short-turn user-facing products; for assistant long-turn, threshold = 3%. If breached, do NOT roll out quantization.
- Soft stop: measured_p95_ms increase > 8% compared to baseline for high-SLO routes. Revert batching window or reduce batch_target.
- Rollout tip: start canary at 1–5% traffic with synthetic warm-ups for cache-driven combos; check live hit rate and quality metrics for 2–4 hours before a gradual ramp.

Microbench pitfalls and debugging checklist
- Spiky arrival patterns amplify negative batching effects: log per-route arrival inter-arrival histogram and include in notes column.
- Cache fragmentation: identical prefixes with small differences (whitespace, ephemeral tokens) will reduce hit-rate; consider normalized prefix fingerprinting.
- Quantization nondeterminism: int4 variants sometimes produce occasional high-probability token shifts — spot-check failing examples and track tokens with KL divergence metric vs float baseline.
- Measurement hygiene: ensure token counters are consistent between runtime metrics and cost accounting (avoid double-counting retries).

Quality evaluation harness (short checklist)
- Create a 200-prompt short-turn set representative of our UI features (few-shot prompts, system instructions, stop tokens).
- Track exact-match on structured outputs and acceptability score on open responses (human or proxy).
- Output fields to compare: BLEU-ish token overlap, top-k token probability drift, human-annotated acceptability for a 100-item sample.

Example row (illustrative numbers)
- run_id: tiny-001
- model: redwood-7b-v2
- hardware: A100-40GB
- seq_len_p50: 32
- seq_len_p95: 96
- arrival_pattern: conversational
- qconfig: int8
- cache_policy: prefix-only
- cache_ttl_secs: 30
- batching_window_ms: 6
- batch_target: 4
- batch_max: 12
- measured_p50_ms: 64
- measured_p95_ms: 138
- measured_tokens: 1_200_000
- total_inference_cost_usd: 42.0
- cost_per_1M_tokens_usd: 35.0
- quality_regression_pct: 0.4
- notes: "Good p50 improvement; p95 stable; cache hit-rate estimate 46% from runtime logs."

Operational suggestions for runtime team
- Expose a per-route micro-config that binds batching window and batch_target. UI teams should be able to opt into "tiny-latency" preset.
- Add lightweight prefix normalization hooks (trim trailing spaces, canonicalize punctuation) before cache keying; measure hit-rate improvement.
- Provide labeled experiment ids in traces so we can line up cost/latency rows to specific config combinations.

Open questions and follow-ups
- How does multi-tenant GPU consolidation impact observed p95 when multiple tiny-latency routes land on same instance? Need a containment test.
- Should we build an automated heuristic that adapts batching_window_ms based on observed inter-arrival percentiles per-minute? (Pro: auto-adapt to traffic; Con: complexity & potential oscillation).
- Determine exact cost model attribution for CPU pre/post-processing (include in total_inference_cost_usd).

Next steps (recommended immediate actions)
- Product-optimize to create the sweep sheet using the column layout above (owner: Aisha).
- Serving-runtime to implement a small-run with the baseline + micro-batch sweep for two models: redwood-7b-v2 and redwood-13b-alt (owner: Miguel).
- Set up a 24-hour combined run for the top 3 combos and produce a short one-page summary with a recommended preset for "tiny-latency" routes.

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep early rollouts conservative: customers notice tiny quality regressions quickly.
- This memo intentionally biases toward short, repeatable sweeps and spreadsheet-first analysis instead of huge design docs.

End.
